paper.title: Romanian Master of Physics 2016 — theory
paper.caveat: The original contains three whole theory problems, seven blank answer sheets, complete worked keys for Q1 and Q2, and a four-page detailed grading scheme for Q3. Printed labels, formulas, values and unit discrepancies are preserved and explained in separate reader notes. The retained key PDF also contains twelve experimental pages without matching questions in this question booklet; those pages remain in the original PDF outside this theory edition.

documentNotes.title: Reader note: native whole tasks and printed footer labels
documentNotes.statement: The original question booklet contains Q1, Compressible fluids (12 requests); Q2, Sources, atoms, and spectra (6 requests); and Theoretical Problem No. 3, “Squeezing” electrical charge carriers using magnetic fields (11 requests). These are three whole problems with 29 connected requests. Q1 and Q2 pages print “Theoretical Problem No. 3” in their recurring footer. The body titles and connected parts establish the problem grouping; the printed footer labels remain in the original PDF.

documentNotes.title: Reader note: retained key authority and original mathematical expressions
documentNotes.statement: The retained solutions_2016.pdf carries Romanian Master of Physics 2016 branding, matching Q1 and Q2 worked keys, and a detailed Q3 grading scheme credited to the named problem authors. It is a key retained by the archive; an organizer publication URL has not been independently verified. The solutions are attributed to the archive. Q1 key equations are small embedded raster images; their printed mathematical content is retained.

documentNotes.title: Reader note: literal flow and shock-key calculations
documentNotes.statement: The B3.1 repeated key stem omits the original question’s condition $v<c$; the condition remains in the question. B3.2 prints $p_s=p+\rho v^2$, $v=276\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and $M=0.802$. Those printed expressions and values are retained. The shock derivation denotes the undisturbed gas by $p,\rho$, while the question uses $p_s,\rho_s$; each source notation remains in its original context.

documentNotes.title: Reader note: literal shock equation and numerical discrepancy
documentNotes.statement: C2.2 prints its final shock-speed factor as $c\sqrt{(x_1y_1-1)/(\gamma x_1-1)}$. C2.3 then prints $341\times0.775=264\ \mathrm{m/s}$ after C2.2 reports Mach 3.58. Those algebraic and numerical forms do not consistently follow the preceding relations. C2.1 prints its final ratio $T_1/T$ without a denominator subscript. These literal source expressions are preserved.

documentNotes.title: Reader note: answer-sheet title correspondence
documentNotes.statement: Question page 9 labels the Sources, atoms, and spectra answer sheet Q3, while the matching question and key label it Q2. The six A/B/C requests, marks and content establish its correspondence to Q2. Both printed labels remain in the transcription and the original answer-sheet crop.

documentNotes.title: Reader note: literal absorption-ratio ordering

It then prints $102.8/97.5=1.054$ and $0.054/n_1^2=1.054/n_2^2-1/(n_2+1)^2$. The printed ratio, search table and both estimates of $A$ are retained literally.

documentNotes.title: Reader note: printed permeability unit and source language
documentNotes.statement: The question prints the magnetic permeability of vacuum as $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$. The unit is dimensionally anomalous for permeability; the printed F is retained. Task 3.iii contains the Romanian word “și” between $\mu$ and $k_B$, also retained.

documentNotes.title: Reader note: complete Q3 rubric and literal source expressions
documentNotes.statement: The matching Q3 key is the complete four-page “Detailed grading scheme”. Every intermediate formula, partial mark, both diagrams and the instruction to credit other correct approaches are retained. The rubric prints $\omega_0\cong5\times10^7\ \mathrm{rotations\,s^{-1}}$, a plus sign between the two component terms of $\vec F_{S.L.}$, its $+e$ potential-energy signs, and the displayed pressure-force differential signs. problems.title: Q1. Compressible fluids

sections.title: A. Bernoulli’s equation
sections.statement: Bernoulli’s equation is the mathematical form of the law of conservation and transformation of energy for a flowing ideal gas. It bears the name of the Swiss physicist Daniel Bernoulli (1700–1782), who derived it in 1738. The easiest way to obtain this equation is to follow a fluid particle (a volume element of the fluid) in its way on a streamline.

parts.label: A
parts.statement: Perform the energy balance between two points in the flowing gas, knowing the parameters $(p_1,\rho_1,v_1)$ and $(p_2,\rho_2,v_2)$, and derive the equation that connects these variables. The adiabatic exponent $\gamma$ of the gas is also known. The parameter $p$ is the gas pressure, $\rho$ its density, and $v$ its speed.

sections.title: B1. Speed of the perturbation
sections.statement:
**B. Propagation of a perturbation in a flowing gas**

If the pressure in a layer of a macroscopically motionless gas system suddenly increases (by heating or rapid compression), the layer will begin to expand, compressing the adjacent layers. This pressure disturbance will be thus transmitted by contiguity as an elastic wave through the gas.

The speed $c$ of this wave is the speed of its wavefront (the most advanced surface, the points of which oscillate in phase and the thermodynamic parameters of which have the same value). If in the reference frame of the unperturbed gas the process of the wave propagation is nonsteady (the gas parameters in any point vary with time), in the reference frame of the wavefront the process will be steady, so the simple equations for a steady state can be applied.

parts.label: B1
parts.statement: Derive the mathematical expression for the speed $c$ of the wavefront, taking into account that the thermodynamic parameters of the unperturbed gas are $(p,\rho)$, while those “behind” the wavefront are $(p_1,\rho_1)=(p+\Delta p,\rho+\Delta\rho)$.

sections.title: B.2 Sound waves
sections.statement: Sound waves are waves of weak disturbances ($\Delta p\ll p$ and $\Delta\rho\ll\rho$) that travel fast enough, their speed being of the order of hundreds of meters per second. Due to this, the gas compressions and rarefactions can be considered as adiabatic, the adiabatic exponent being $\gamma$.

parts.label: B2
parts.statement: Using the result from B1, obtain the mathematical expression for the sound speed in the gas and, using Bernoulli’s eq., derive the relation between the flow speed at a given point in the gas and the local sound speed.

sections.title: B.3 Mach’s number
sections.statement:
For classifying the speed performances of bodies in a fluid (e.g. aircrafts), as well as the flow regimes of fluids, the Swiss aeronautical engineer Jakob Ackeret (1898–1981) — one of the leading authorities in the 20th century aeronautics — proposed in 1929 that the ratio of the body or of the fluid’s speed $v$ and the local sound speed $c$ in that fluid to be called Mach’s number

$$M=\frac vc,$$

after the name of the great Czech (then in the Austrian empire) physicist and philosopher Ernst Mach (1838–1916). Primarily, the value of this non-dimensional quantity delimitates the incompressible from the compressible behavior of a flowing fluid, in aeronautics this limit being settled to $M=0.3$.

parts.label: B3.1
parts.statement: Find the relative variation of the gas density as a function of Mach’s number, when its motion is slowed down to a stop, its initial velocity being $v<c$, and calculate its maximum value for a flow to be considered incompressible.

parts.label: B3.2
parts.statement: The pressure at the nose of an aircraft in flight was found to be $1.92\cdot10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$ and the speed of air relative to the aircraft was zero at this point. The pressure and temperature of the undisturbed air were $1.01\cdot10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$ and $21.1\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm C$ respectively. The adiabatic exponent for this temperature is $\gamma=1.40$. Find the speed and the Mach number of the aircraft.

parts.label: B3.3
parts.statement: When a gas is flowing through a pipe, it exerts a friction force on the fluid, which is not always negligible. If at the entrance of such a pipe the static pressure in the flowing fluid is $p_1=6.90\cdot10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$ and the Mach number is $M_1=0.700$, while at the exit $M_2=1$, find the expression and the numerical value of the force with which the fluid is acting on the pipe. The adiabatic exponent is $\gamma=1.40$, the constant cross section of the pipe is $S=9.29\cdot10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^2}$, and the relative increase of the gas temperature through the pipe is $\Delta T/T_1=5\cdot10^{-3}$.

sections.title: C.1 The shock adiabat
sections.statement:
**C. Shock waves**

There are two types of acoustic waves in a gas: sound waves and shock waves. The latter appear when a body moves in a gas with a supersonic speed (i.e. the relative speed of the body with respect to that of the gas is greater than the sound speed). At supersonic speeds, in front of the body appears a very thin layer of gas with a higher pressure, called compression shock. This kind of special acoustic waves were studied by Mach, so the envelope of such a wave is known as Mach’s cone, having the body in its apex. Passing through the compression shock, the thermodynamic parameters of the gas change abruptly. The Mach’s cone is an example of an oblique shock, but we are interested here mainly in normal shocks, for which the shock wavefront is perpendicular on the body or fluid velocity.

For shock waves the pressure/density differences between the two sides of the wavefront can reach very high values. Passing through the wavefront, the thermodynamic parameters vary abruptly, with a sudden jump. This is another reason for which a shock wavefront is called a pressure or a compression shock.

The gas compressed by the shock wave undergoes an irreversible adiabatic process which cannot be described by Poisson’s equation. However, an equation for the shock adiabat was deduced towards the end of the XIXth century by the Scottish physicist William Rankine (1820–1872) and, independently by him, by the French engineer Pierre Henri Hugoniot (1851–1887), using the mass and energy conservation, as well as the momentum equation. The Rankine–Hugoniot equation, or the shock adiabat, relates the pressure and the density of the gas compressed by a shock wave.

parts.label: C1
parts.statement:
Denoting with $p_s$ and $\rho_s$ the gas pressure and density in front of the compression shock (which are known), and with $p_1$ and $\rho_1$ the same parameters behind the shock (which are unknown), show that the pressure ratio $y_1=p_1/p_s$ is related with the density ratio $x_1=\rho_1/\rho_s$ by a relation of the form

$$y_1=\frac{\alpha x_1-\beta}{\tau-\sigma x_1}.$$

Find the explicit form of the coefficients $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\tau$ and $\sigma$.

The adiabatic exponent $\gamma$ of the gas is known.

*Note: For simplicity, use a stream tube with a constant cross section, crossing perpendicularly the wavefront of the normal shock.*

sections.title: C.2 A shockwave created by an explosion
sections.statement: An explosion creates a spherically shockwave propagating radially into still air at $p_s=1.01\cdot10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$ and $t_s=20.0\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm C$. A recording instrument registers a maximum pressure of $p_1=1.48\cdot10^6\ \mathrm{Pa}$ as the shock wavefront passes by. The adiabatic coefficient of air for this compression shock is $\gamma=1.38$, the molar mass of air is $\mu=29\ \mathrm{g/mol}$ and the ideal gas constant is $R=8.32\ \mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$.

parts.label: C2.1
parts.statement: Determine the air temperature increase $T_1/T_s$ under the action of the compression shock.

parts.label: C2.2
parts.statement: Determine the Mach’s number corresponding to the speed of the shockwave.

parts.label: C2.3
parts.statement: Determine the wind’s speed $v_1$ following the shock wavefront, with respect to a fixed observer.

parts.label: C2.4
parts.statement:
During the compression shock the gas temperature and pressure sharply increase, much more than in a quasistatic adiabatic compression. After the shock, the gas expands adiabatically, but because the slope of the adiabatic process is smaller than that of the adiabatic shock, when the gas density reaches again the initial value, its pressure is still higher than that of the unperturbed gas, $p_s$.

Derive the ratios $p_2/p_s$ and $T_2/T_s$ at the end of the expansion process and calculate the numerical values of $p_2$ and $T_2$.

parts.label: C2.5
parts.statement:
From this point the gas is cooling until it reaches the initial state. Assuming that for the entire cyclic process the adiabatic exponent has the same value, derive an expression for the entropy variation of the mass unit of air during the compression shock and calculate its numerical value.

solution.statement:
## A. Bernoulli’s equation — 1.5 p

**Solution.** The law of conservation and transformation of energy is the first law of thermodynamics. Since the processes taking place inside the gas are adiabatic, this law has the form

$$W+\Delta E=0,$$

where the work done by the gas is

$$W=p_2\Delta V_2-p_1\Delta V_1=\Delta m\left(\frac{p_2}{\rho_2}-\frac{p_1}{\rho_1}\right)$$

and the variation of the total energy of the gas is

$$\Delta E=\Delta K+\Delta U=\frac{\Delta m}{2}(v_2^2-v_1^2)+\Delta m\,c_V(T_2-T_1),$$

so that

$$\frac{v_1^2}{2}+\frac{p_1}{\rho_1}+c_VT_1=\frac{v_2^2}{2}+\frac{p_2}{\rho_2}+c_VT_2.$$

Making use of the Robert Mayer eq., $c_p-c_V=R/\mu$, and of $c_p/c_V=\gamma$, we find $c_V=R/[\mu(\gamma-1)]$. With the Clapeyron–Mendeleev eq., $T=p\mu/(\rho R)$, the energy conservation eq. becomes

$$\boxed{\frac{v_1^2}{2}+\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}\frac{p_1}{\rho_1}=\frac{v_2^2}{2}+\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}\frac{p_2}{\rho_2}}.$$

## B. Propagation of a perturbation in a flowing gas — 4 p

### B1. Speed of the perturbation — 1.5 p

**Solution.** In the reference frame of the undisturbed gas (laboratory frame, see Fig.1), the speed of the gas in front of the wavefront (to the right) is $v=0$ and the speed of the gas behind the wavefront (to the left) is $v_1<c$.

In the reference frame moving together with the wavefront, the speed of the undisturbed gas laying in front of the wavefront is $u=v-c=-c$ (the undisturbed gas runs against the wavefront) and the gas behind (to the left) the wavefront (or in the wakefield, or even upstream), which is still compressed, moves to the left with the speed $u_1=v_1-c<0$.

![Fig.1 laboratory reference frame and wavefront reference frame](p1-k-wavefront)

The continuity eq. (mass flow rate) is

$$\Phi=\frac{\delta m}{\delta t}=\rho S\frac{\delta x}{\delta t}=\rho Sv=\mathrm{const.}$$

so for a stream tube of constant cross section

$$\rho u=\rho_1u_1.$$

The momentum eq. (Newton’s second law) is

$$\vec F=\frac{\Delta\vec P}{\Delta t},$$

or

$$(p-p_1)S=\frac{\delta m(u_1-u)}{\delta t}=\Phi(u_1-u)=\rho_1Su_1^2-\rho Su^2.$$

Hence $p+\rho u^2=p_1+\rho_1u_1^2$. Using these eqs. (eliminating $u_1$), we find

$$\boxed{c=|u|=\sqrt{\frac{p_1-p}{\rho(1-\rho/\rho_1)}}=\sqrt{\left(1+\frac{\Delta\rho}{\rho}\right)\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta\rho}}}.$$

### B2. Sound waves — 0.5 p

**Solution.**

$$c=\sqrt{\frac{\Delta p(\rho+\Delta\rho)}{\rho\Delta\rho}}\approx\sqrt{\frac{\Delta p\rho}{\rho\Delta\rho}}=\sqrt{\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta\rho}}.$$

Since for an adiabatic process $p\rho^{-\gamma}=\mathrm{const.}$, we find

$$c=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma p}{\rho}}.$$

Under these circumstances, Bernoulli’s eq. can be rewritten as

$$\boxed{\frac{v_1^2}{2}+\frac{c_1^2}{\gamma-1}=\frac{v_2^2}{2}+\frac{c_2^2}{\gamma-1}}.$$

### B3.1 — 0.5 p

**Solution.** In this case Bernoulli’s eq. becomes

$$\frac{v^2}{2}+\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}\frac p\rho=\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}\frac{p+\Delta p}{\rho+\Delta\rho}.$$

Taking into account that $c=\sqrt{\Delta p/\Delta\rho}=\sqrt{\gamma p/\rho}$, we find

$$\boxed{\frac{\Delta\rho}{\rho}=\frac{M^2}{2-M^2}}.$$

For a flow to be considered incompressible, the relative variation of density should not exceed

$$\left(\frac{\Delta\rho}{\rho}\right)_{\max}=4.71\cdot10^{-2}=5\%.$$

### B3.2 — 0.5 p

**Solution.** Applying Bernoulli’s eq. we find the stagnation pressure $p_s$ of air at the nose of the aircraft is

$$p_s=p+\rho v^2,$$

so

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{p_s-p}{\rho}}=\sqrt{\left(\frac{p_s}{p}-1\right)\frac{RT}{\mu}}=276\ \mathrm{m/s}.$$

The sound speed in air is

$$c=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT}{\mu}}=344\ \mathrm{m/s},$$

the Mach’s number being $M=v/c=0.802$.

### B3.3 — 1.0 p

**Solution.** From the momentum eq. the force exerted by the gas on the pipe is

$$\begin{aligned}
F_f&=S[(p_1+\rho_1v_1^2)-(p_2+\rho_2v_2^2)]\\
&=S[(p_1+\rho_1c_1^2M_1^2)-(p_2+\rho_2c_2^2M_2^2)]\\
&=S[(p_1+\gamma p_1M_1^2)-(p_2+\gamma p_2M_2^2)]\\
&=S[p_1(1+\gamma M_1^2)-p_2(1+\gamma M_2^2)].
\end{aligned}$$

From the Clapeyron–Mendeleev eq. $p_1/p_2=\rho_1T_1/(\rho_2T_2)$, while from continuity $\rho_1v_1=\rho_2v_2$, or

$$M_1\sqrt{p_1\rho_1}=M_2\sqrt{p_2\rho_2}.$$

Using the above eqs. it follows that

$$p_2=\frac{M_1p_1}{M_2}\sqrt{\frac{T_2}{T_1}}.$$

Hence

$$\begin{aligned}
F_f&=p_1S\left[(1+\gamma M_1^2)-\frac{M_1}{M_2}\sqrt{\frac{T_2}{T_1}}(1+\gamma M_2^2)\right]\\
&=p_1S\left[(1+\gamma M_1^2)-\frac{M_1}{M_2}\sqrt{\frac{T_1+\Delta T}{T_1}}(1+\gamma M_2^2)\right]\\
&=p_1S\left[(1+\gamma M_1^2)-\frac{M_1}{M_2}\sqrt{1+\frac{\Delta T}{T_1}}(1+\gamma M_2^2)\right],
\end{aligned}$$

with a numerical value of $F_f=116\ \mathrm N$.

## C. Shock waves — 4.5 p

### C1. The shock adiabat — 1.5 p

**Solution.** The repeated key stem denotes the known undisturbed quantities by $p,\rho$. In the reference frame moving with the shock the processes are steady. If, in the laboratory frame, $v$ is the velocity of the body passing through the stationary gas, which is also the speed of the compression shock, and $v_1$ that of the gas behind the compression shock, then in the shock reference frame the speed of the undisturbed gas will be $u=-v$, while that of the gas behind the shock will be $u_1=v_1-v<0$.

Since there are three unknown variables, $u_1,p_1$ and $\rho_1$, we need three equations to solve the problem:

- The mass conservation eq. (the mass flow rate eq.), for a stream tube with a constant cross section passing perpendicularly through the normal shock: $\rho u=\rho_1u_1$.
- The momentum equation: $p+\rho u^2=p_1+\rho_1u_1^2$.
- The energy conservation equation (Bernoulli eq.):

$$\frac{u^2}{2}+\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}\frac p\rho=\frac{u_1^2}{2}+\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}\frac{p_1}{\rho_1}.$$

Using these eqs. (eliminating $u_1$), we find

$$\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{\rho u^2}{p}=\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma-1}\frac{x_1}{\frac{\gamma+1}{\gamma-1}-x_1},\\
\displaystyle\frac{p_1}{p}=1+\frac{\rho u^2}{p}\left(1-\frac1{x_1}\right).
\end{cases}$$

Hence

$$\boxed{y_1=\frac{\frac{\gamma+1}{\gamma-1}x_1-1}{\frac{\gamma+1}{\gamma-1}-x_1}}.$$

This is the shock adiabat equation. Consequently, the requested coefficients are $\alpha=\tau=(\gamma+1)/(\gamma-1)$ and $\beta=\sigma=1$.

### C2.1 — 0.5 p

**Solution.** From the shock adiabat $y_1=(\alpha x_1-1)/(\alpha-x_1)$ it follows that $x_1=(\alpha y_1+1)/(\alpha+y_1)$, where $y_1=p_1/p_s=14.7$ and $\alpha=(\gamma+1)/(\gamma-1)=6.26$. Hence $\rho_1/\rho_s=4.44$.

Since $T_s=293\ \mathrm K$, the still air density is given by the Clapeyron–Mendeleev eq.,

$$\rho_s=\frac{p_s}{(R/\mu)T_s}=1.20\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}.$$

Under these circumstances, the air density behind the shock wavefront is $\rho_1=5.33\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$, so the temperature behind the shock is

$$T_1=\frac{p_1\mu}{\rho_1R}=968\ \mathrm K,\quad\text{or }t_1=695\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm C,$$

the temperature ratio being $T_1/T=3.30$ (the last denominator is printed without the subscript in this key line).

### C2.2 — 0.5 p

**Solution.** From the above eqs. it follows that

$$c_{sh}=\sqrt{\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_s}\frac{p_1-p_s}{\rho_1-\rho_s}}=\sqrt{\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_s}\frac{\frac{p_1}{p_s}-1}{\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_s}-1}\frac p{\rho_s}}=c\sqrt{\frac{x_1y_1-1}{\gamma x_1-1}},$$

or $M=3.58$.

### C2.3 — 0.5 p

**Solution.**

$$v_1=v-|u_1|=c_{sh}\left(1-\frac{\rho_s}{\rho_1}\right)=341\cdot0.775=264\ \mathrm{m/s}.$$

### C2.4 — 0.5 p

**Solution.** At the end of the adiabatic expansion the requested ratios are

$$\frac{p_2}{p_1}=\left(\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}\right)^\gamma=\left(\frac{\rho_s}{\rho_1}\right)^\gamma=\left(\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_s}\right)^{-\gamma}$$

and

$$\frac{T_2}{T_1}=\frac{p_2\mu/(\rho_sR)}{p_1\mu/(\rho_1R)}=\frac{p_2\rho_1}{p_1\rho_s}.$$

Since

$$\frac{p_1}{p_s}=\frac{\frac{\gamma+1}{\gamma-1}\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_s}-1}{\frac{\gamma+1}{\gamma-1}-\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_s}},$$

then

$$\frac{p_2}{p_s}=\frac{\frac{\gamma+1}{\gamma-1}\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_s}-1}{\frac{\gamma+1}{\gamma-1}-\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_s}}\left(\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_s}\right)^{-\gamma}=1.66$$

and

$$\frac{T_2}{T_s}=\frac{p_2\mu/(\rho_sR)}{p_s\mu/(\rho_sR)}=\frac{p_2}{p_s}=1.66.$$

So $p_2=1.68\cdot10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$ and $T_2=486\ \mathrm K$ ($t_2=213\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm C$).

### C2.5 — 1.0 p

**Solution.**

![Fig.2 pressure-density cycle for compression shock, adiabatic expansion and isochoric cooling](p1-k-cycle)

Admitting that the cycle is enclosed by an isochoric process, since the entropy variation during the entire cycle, as well as for the adiabatic expansion are zero, then

$$\frac{\Delta S_{shock}}{\Delta m}=-\frac{\Delta S_V}{\Delta m}=-\frac{C_V}{\mu}\ln\frac{T_s}{T_2}=\frac1{\gamma-1}\frac R\mu\ln\frac{T_2}{T_s}=383\ \mathrm{J/(kg\,K)}.$$

The printed key’s numerical and algebraic forms above are retained literally; source discrepancies are described separately in the reader notes.

sections.title: A. Light source
sections.statement: In its proper reference frame, a point source emits light in the form of a divergent conical beam, with the angular width of $90^{\circ}$ (from $-45^{\circ}$ to $+45^{\circ}$ with respect to the cone axis). In a reference frame which moves towards the source with an unknown speed $v$, the angular width of the beam is of only $60^{\circ}$ (from $-30^{\circ}$ to $+30^{\circ}$ with respect to the same cone axis). The light speed in vacuum is $c=2.998\cdot10^8\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

parts.label: A
parts.statement: Determine the speed $v$ of the source.

sections.title: B. Balmer emission spectrum
sections.statement:
The spectral resolving power of a spectrometer is $R=5\cdot10^5$. The spectrometer is used to observe the Balmer series in the emission spectrum of the hydrogen atom (the visible domain).

*Note: The possible mechanisms of broadening of the spectral lines (Lorentzian, Gaussian, etc.) will not be considered.*

parts.label: B.1
parts.statement: Express the mathematical definition of the spectral resolving power of the instrument.

parts.label: B.2
parts.statement: Determine the highest value for the principal quantum number $n$ of the energy level for which the spectral line emitted by an atom for the transition to the level $n'=2$ can still be distinctly resolved by the instrument, with respect with its neighbours.

sections.title: C. Absorption spectra
sections.statement: The energy levels of an atom are given by $E_n=-A/n^2$, where $n$ is an integer and $A$ is a positive constant. Among the adjacent spectral lines which, at room temperature, the atom can absorb, two have the wavelengths $97.5\ \mathrm{nm}$ and $102.8\ \mathrm{nm}$, respectively. The elementary electric charge is $e=1.602\cdot10^{-19}\ \mathrm C$, the speed of light in vacuum is $c=2.998\cdot10^8\ \mathrm{m/s}$, and Planck’s constant is $h=6.626\cdot10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$.

parts.label: C.1
parts.statement: Find the values of the quantum numbers $n$ of the energy levels implied in the transitions.

parts.label: C.2
parts.statement: Determine the value of the constant $A$ in joule and in electron-volt.

parts.label: C.3
parts.statement:
Identify the nature of the atom and justify the choice made.

solution.statement:
Q2. Sources, atoms, and spectra — proposed by prof. Florea ULIU, PhD, University of Craiova.

## A. Light source — 2.50 p

### 1st Solution

Starting from the Lorentz transformations it is easy to obtain the so-called formula for the aberration of light

$$\tan\frac\phi2=\sqrt{\frac{1-v/c}{1+v/c}}\tan\frac{\phi'}2,$$

so that

$$v=c\frac{\tan^2(\phi'/2)-\tan^2(\phi/2)}{\tan^2(\phi'/2)+\tan^2(\phi/2)}.$$

With $\phi=30^{\circ}$ and $\phi'=45^{\circ}$, it follows immediately that $v/c=0.4098$, or $v=1.229\cdot10^8\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

### 2nd Solution

This solution is based on the transformation relations for velocities. Let $x'$ and $x$ be the axes of the cone in the proper reference frame, $K'$ and the other one, $K$. The velocity of $K'$ with respect to $K$ is $v$. Consider a photon moving on the external surface of the cone with the apex angle of $90^{\circ}$ and with $x'$ as a symmetry axis. Then $v_x'=c\cos45^{\circ}=c/\sqrt2$. The other component has the same value $v_y'=c\sin45^{\circ}=c/\sqrt2$. The speed $v_x$ in reference frame $K$ is given by the transformation law

$$v_x=\frac{v+v_x'}{1+vv_x'/c^2}=\frac{v+c/\sqrt2}{1+vc/(c^2\sqrt2)}=c\frac{c+v\sqrt2}{v+c\sqrt2}.\tag{*}$$

Applying the other transformation law (for the $y$, respectively $y'$ components of the velocities), we will get

$$v_y=v_y'\frac{\sqrt{1-(v/c)^2}}{1+vv_x'/c^2}=\frac c{\sqrt2}\frac{\sqrt{1-(v/c)^2}}{1+v/(c\sqrt2)}.\tag{**}$$

*Note: This expression for $v_y$ could be obtained from $v_y=\sqrt{c^2-v_x^2}$, with $v_x$ given by eq.(*). Here it was taken into account that the photon moves with the same speed, $c$, both in $K'$, as well as in $K$.*

From $\tan30^{\circ}=v_y/v_x=1/\sqrt3$, using eqs.(*) and (**), it follows that

$$v=c\frac{\sqrt3-\sqrt2}{2-\sqrt{3/2}}=0.4100c,$$

or $v=1.229\cdot10^8\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

### 3rd Solution

This method uses directly the Lorentz transformations, written in differential form. So,

$$\Delta x=\gamma(\Delta x'+v\Delta t')\quad\text{and}\quad\Delta y=\Delta y'.\tag{***}$$

Consider a photon moving on the external surface of the cone, in the reference frame $K'$. If this photon correlates two events having a spatial separation $\Delta x'$ on the $x'$ axis, their spatial separation on the $y'$ axis is $\Delta y'=\Delta x'$ (because the moving direction of the photon makes $45^{\circ}$ with the axis $x'$). The time interval separating the events is $\Delta t'=\Delta x'/c_x$, with $c_x=c/\sqrt2$. Thus $\Delta t'=\Delta x'\sqrt2/c$. [It could be reasoned considering that the photon moves with the speed $c$ on a distance $\Delta x'\sqrt2$.]

Now, eq.(***) takes the form

$$\Delta x=\gamma\left(\Delta x'+v\frac{\sqrt2}{c}\Delta x'\right)=\gamma\Delta x'\left(1+\frac{v\sqrt2}{c}\right),\quad\Delta y=\Delta x',$$

respectively. Knowing that $\tan30^{\circ}=\Delta y/\Delta x=1/\sqrt3$ and using the usual notation $\beta=v/c$, the resulting eq. is

$$5\beta^2+2\sqrt2\beta-2=0,$$

the physical solution of which is $\beta=0.41$. So $v=c\beta=0.4101c$, obtaining the same result as above.

## B. Balmer emission spectrum

### B.1 — 0.25 p

**Solution.** The spectral resolving power of an optical instrument is $R=\lambda/\Delta\lambda$, where $\Delta\lambda$ is the minimum value of the difference between the wavelengths of two adjacent spectral lines, $\lambda$ and $\lambda+\Delta\lambda$, which can be distinctly observed with the instrument. According to the Rayleigh criterion, this spectral (chromatic) interval corresponds to the following situation: the first zero minimum beside the principal maximum of the radiation $\lambda$ coincides with the principal maximum of the same order of the radiation $\lambda+\Delta\lambda$.

### B.2 — 2.25 p

**Solution.** The wavelengths of Balmer Series (the only series in visible) are given by

$$\frac1\lambda=K\left(\frac14-\frac1{n^2}\right),$$

where $K$ is a positive constant (the value of which is not important now) and the quantum number $n$ can take the values $3,4,5,\ldots$. The variation $\Delta\lambda$ of the wavelength $\lambda$ must be found when the quantum number $n$ varies with one unit (i.e. $\Delta n=1$). The approximation $\Delta\lambda/\Delta n\approx d\lambda/dn$ (as if $n$ would vary continuously) can be used. The derivative of Balmer eq. gives

$$-\frac1{\lambda^2}\frac{d\lambda}{dn}=\frac{2K}{n^3},\quad\text{so}\quad\frac{d\lambda}{dn}=-\frac{2K}{n^3}\lambda^2.$$

Using this result, we can tell that the ratio $\Delta\lambda/\lambda$ when $\Delta n=1$ is given by

$$\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda}\approx\frac{2K}{n^3}\lambda=\frac2{n^3}\left(\frac14-\frac1{n^2}\right)^{-1}.$$

The minus sign was abandoned because we will consider only positive variations of $\Delta\lambda$.

According to the definition, the spectral resolving power of an instrument is given by $R\equiv\lambda/\Delta\lambda$. In this case

$$\frac\lambda{\Delta\lambda}=\frac{n^3}{2}\left(\frac14-\frac1{n^2}\right)=\frac{n^3}{8}-\frac n2.$$

Asking this value to be smaller than the value of $R$ given in the text, it follows that $n^3/8-n/2<R$. Knowing that $R=5\cdot10^5$, we can conclude that the highest value of $n$ is pretty big. Consequently, ignoring the second term in the left hand side of the above inequality, we get $n<158.7$. The physical solution is $n_{\lim}=158$.

## C. Absorption spectra

### C.1 — 3.00 p

An absorption line corresponds to an excited state of the atom, or to a down (quantum number $n_1$)–up (quantum number $n_2>n_1$) transition. For such a transition to happen it is necessary to transmit the atom an energy

$$W(n_1\to n_2)=\frac A{n_1^2}-\frac A{n_2^2}.$$

If it is a photoexcitation, the wavelength of the absorbed radiation has the value

$$\lambda(n_1\to n_2)=\frac{ch}{A}\left(\frac1{n_1^2}-\frac1{n_2^2}\right)^{-1}.$$

The adjacent absorption lines must correspond to the transitions $n_1\to n_2$ and $n_1\to n_2+1$. The last transition needs more energy, so it will correspond to a smaller wavelength. The constant $A$ being unknown, we will derive the ratio of those two wavelengths:

$$\frac{\lambda(n_1\to n_2)}{\lambda(n_1\to n_2+1)}=\frac{\frac1{n_1^2}-\frac1{n_2^2}}{\frac1{n_1^2}-\frac1{(n_2+1)^2}}=\frac{102.8}{97.5}=1.054.$$

To solve this eq. we will write it first in the form

$$\frac{0.054}{n_1^2}=\frac{1.054}{n_2^2}-\frac1{(n_2+1)^2},$$

and will try, progressively, the possible values $n_2=2,3,4,5,\ldots$. For $n_1$, the obtained results will be:

| $n_2$ | $n_1$ |
| --- | --- |
| 2 | 0.59528 |
| 3 | $0.99439\approx1$ |
| 4 | 1.44463 |
| 5 | 1.93769 |
| 6 | 2.46743 |

and so on. Analyzing these values, the conclusion is that the absorption has as a consequence the transition from level $n_1=1$ to the level $n_2=3$ (the other values found for $n_1$ being far from integer values).

### C.2 — 1.50 p

On one hand, with $\lambda(1\to3)=102.8\ \mathrm{nm}$, we get

$$A=\frac{ch}{\lambda(1\to3)}[1/1-1/9]^{-1}=2.174\cdot10^{-18}\ \mathrm J.\qquad\text{1.00 p}$$

From the formula containing $\lambda(1\to4)=97.5\ \mathrm{nm}$, the result will be

$$A=\frac{ch}{\lambda(1\to4)}[1/1-1/16]^{-1}=2.173\cdot10^{-18}\ \mathrm J,$$

which is practically the same result. Transforming the result in electron-volt, the result reads

$$A=2.1735\cdot10^{-18}\ \mathrm J=\frac{2.1735\cdot10^{-18}}{1.602\cdot10^{-19}}=13.57\ \mathrm{eV}.\qquad\text{0.50 p}$$

### C.3 — 0.50 p

Since the ionization energy for the hydrogen atom from its fundamental state is $13.6\ \mathrm{eV}$, the conclusion is that the atom is hydrogen.

problems.title: Theoretical Problem No.3. “Squeezing” electrical charge carriers using magnetic fields
problems.statement:
Plasma physics has to solve the problem of achieving devices capable of producing energy on a large scale through fusion. There are no issues related to the feasibility of the scientific method — the process can be observed as it happens in stars. But there are many technological feasibility problems primarily related to heating the plasma, and controlling it, at temperatures like the ones in the Sun. Physical conditions of the nuclear fusion cannot be achieved in containers. Maintaining plasma localized in limited volume can be accomplished using magnetic fields.

The first two tasks of the problem require analyzing several situations in which the movement of charged particles is limited by external magnetic fields. The third task asks you to study the confinement of electrical charge carriers through their own magnetic field. When solving the problem you may rely on the following numerical values: elementary electric charge $e=1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm C$, mass of the electron $m=9.1\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$, the magnetic permeability of vacuum $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$.

The permeability unit above is retained as printed in the question; see the separate reader note.

sections.title: Task No.1
sections.statement:
A very long metallic cylinder (a perfect electric conductor), having the length $L$ and the radius $R$, $(L\gg R)$ rotates at constant angular speed $\omega$ around its axis of symmetry.

The cylinder is located in a homogeneous magnetic field whose induction $\vec B$ is parallel to the axis of symmetry of the cylinder. The mass of electron is $m$ and his electric charge is $-e$. Let the dielectric permittivity of the material from which the cylinder is made be $\varepsilon$.

parts.label: 1.i
parts.statement: For a stationary situation determine the expression of the bulk density of electric charge $\rho$ into the cylinder at a distance $r$ from its axis of symmetry $(0<r<R)$. Express the result as function of $B,e,m,\omega$ and $\varepsilon$.

parts.label: 1.ii
parts.statement: Determine the expression of angular velocity $\omega_0$ so that the bulk charge density is zero at any point of the cylinder. Express the result as function of $B,e$ and $m$.

parts.label: 1.iii
parts.statement: Evaluate the possibility of the practical realization of a zero bulk charge density in any point of the metallic cylinder, when an experiment of the type described in question is carried out in the Earth’s magnetic field in a place where the magnetic field induction is $B=1.82\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm T$. Briefly argue the answer.

sections.title: Task No.2
sections.statement:
In a vacuum chamber there is a long, straight wire of negligible thickness made from a material with high electrical conductivity. An electrical current with the intensity of $I=10\ \mathrm A$ passes through the wire.

Electrons are sent on a direction perpendicular on the wire, towards the wire. Their motion starts at the distance $r_0$ from the wire, with an initial speed $v_0$ much smaller than speed of light. The electrons cannot approach the wire at a distance less than $r_0/2$. Consider two reference frames — one being the laboratory system S.L. and the other being a mobile system S.M. that runs parallel to the wire with a constant speed $v_0$ in the direction in which the current flows through the wire.

Neglect the magnetic field of Earth.

parts.label: 2.i
parts.statement: Deduce the expressions of induction of the magnetic field produced by the current flowing through the wire in each of the two reference frames $\vec B_{S.L.}(r)$, $\vec B_{S.M.}(r)$.

parts.label: 2.ii
parts.statement: Determine the expression of the difference between Lorentz forces in the two reference systems, $\vec F_{S.L.}(r)-\vec F_{S.M.}(r)$, forces acting on the electron sent to the wire. Express the result in terms of $e,\mu_0,I,r$ and $v_0$.

parts.label: 2.iii
parts.statement: State the values of the electron velocity’s $\vec v(r_0/2)$ components in both reference frames.

parts.label: 2.iv
parts.statement: Determine the expression of the speed $v_0$ as function of $e,m,I,\mu_0$. Calculate the numerical value of $v_0$.

parts.label: 2.v
parts.statement: Deduce the expression of the maximum distance from the wire $D$ at which one can find the electron, as function of $r_0$, when the electron moves away from wire on a direction perpendicular on it.

sections.title: Task No.3
sections.statement:
A cylindrical column of plasma having the radius $R$ and the length $L$ is generated in a vacuum chamber. The plasma appears as result of ionization of a gas, such that the concentrations of electrons $n_e(r)$ and ions $n_i(r)$ are equal at every point $n_i(r)=n_e(r)=n(r)$; the common value $n(r)$ depends only on the distance between the point and the axis of symmetry of the plasma cylinder. It is assumed that the plasma is in a stationary state, and therefore all its macroscopic characteristics are independent on time. It may be admitted that the temperature $T$ of plasma is the same at every point of the column and that at these temperature the parameters describing plasma abide the perfect gas law. The electric charge of electron is $-e$ and the ions are monovalent, carrying an electric charge $e$. Consider as known the magnetic permeability of plasma $\mu$ and Boltzmann’s constant $k_B$. Between the electrodes at the ends of the plasma column passes through the plasma an electrical current characterized by a constant density $j(r)=j$.

Consider an elementary portion of the hollow cylinder having the radiuses $r$ and $r+dr$ as in joined figure. Elementary portion has a height equal to the unit. In the annulus (circular crown) representing the cross section of the plasma column the elementary portion covers the angle $d\varphi$.

![Original elementary plasma annulus of height1, radii r and r plus dr, and angle dphi](p3-q-plasma)

parts.label: 3.i
parts.statement: Write the expressions of the forces acting on this elementary volume of plasma ($\vec F_p$ due to pressure $p(r)$ in the column of plasma, $\vec F_e$ due to the interaction with electrical charges carriers that there are in plasma, $\vec F_m$ due to the interaction with magnetic field of electrical current flowing through plasma). Write the equation describing the equilibrium of the considered elementary portion of plasma.

parts.label: 3.ii
parts.statement: Deduce the expression of pressure $p(r)$ in a point of the column of plasma. Express the answer as function of $r,j,R$ and magnetic permeability $\mu$.

parts.label: 3.iii
parts.statement:
Determine the expression of the number of particles $N$ carrying electrical charge in the column of plasma as function of $L,I,T,\mu$ și $k_B$.

© Topic proposed by: Dr. Delia DAVIDESCU; Dr. Adrian DAFINEI.
